name: Ben Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Valley Care Co-operative, which is owned by the carers, so I'm technically one of my own bosses, for all the good it does my bank balance. I'm the senior on the dementia round, eight or nine houses spread up the valley, and I train the new starters by taking them out with me. A day is a lot of driving on single-track roads, a lot of tea, and a lot of patience with people who don't remember you from yesterday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment someone with dementia relaxes because your voice feels familiar, even if your name doesn't. What wears me out is the car: it's fourteen years old, and every rattle sounds like a bill. Sam, my boyfriend, is a teaching assistant at the village primary, and between us we pay the rent and the fuel and that's about it. We've got maybe three weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but nicely. At the co-op meeting I'd say the hype was never going to give Mrs Pryce her bath. Online I'd probably share a funny meme and get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means life stays tight but steady. The co-op isn't rich, but nobody's getting rich off my clients either, and that's why I stay. Out here the nearest other care job is forty minutes over the hill, so I'm not going anywhere anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the dementia round and keep training the new starters, same as now. I'd try the voice notes thing the co-op is testing, where you talk into your phone in the car and it writes up the visit, because that would give me twenty minutes back a day. And Sam and I would keep trying to get the savings up to two months, which we never quite manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, a bit relieved. Mostly I'd be thinking about the car's MOT, the yearly safety test, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd try the voice notes. Do you use AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. Sam showed me how to use a chatbot to write a gentle message to a family when their mum's getting worse, because I'm bad at finding the words in writing. I always change it before I send it, but it gets me started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those twenty minutes a day go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, probably on Mr Jones, who walks to the bus stop every afternoon looking for a bus that stopped running in 1990. If I've got twenty minutes, I can walk him back slowly instead of rushing him. That's the bit of the job nobody pays for.

say: The **hype** was never going to give my clients their bath.
I'd share a joke online and **get back to work**.
think: Life stays **tight but steady** in the co-op.
The nearest other care job is **forty minutes** over the hill, so I'm staying anyway.
do: Keep the **dementia round** and keep training new starters.
Try the co-op's **voice notes** in the car to save twenty minutes a day.
Keep trying to lift savings to **two months** with Sam.
feel: **Flat** and a bit relieved, with the car's yearly test on his mind.
S0.quote: The co-op isn't rich, but nobody's getting rich off my clients either, and that's why I stay.
fieldNote: He values the **co-op** for its fairness more than for its pay.
His real worries are the **old car** and three weeks of savings, not AI.
He'd spend saved time on **slow care**, like walking a client home.

steps.text: Keep the dementia round and keep training the new starters
Use the co-op's voice notes app to write visits up in the car
Try to get joint savings up to two months with Sam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say carers are fine and everyone should calm down, which is half true. At the co-op I'd say if software saves us money, the money goes into wages and not into a fancy office. Online I'd share the union's line about paperwork going to machines and time going back to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd be fine, but Sam might not be. His school is already trying out an AI reading tutor, and if that works, they'll need fewer teaching assistants. My job is hands and kettles, so the robots are years off for me, but our rent is two wages, not one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new rota and notes system properly, so I can teach the new starters on it, because somebody has to. I'd put a motion to the co-op's general meeting that any money saved by the software goes into paid travel time. And I'd sit down with Sam and work out what we'd cut if his hours dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like watching the weather over someone else's field and knowing it'll reach yours later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut if Sam's hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gym first, then the streaming, then Sam's evening class in Spanish, which would break his heart. We'd keep the car going whatever happens, because without it I can't work at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said carers are fine, but that's only half true. What's the other half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other half is that the office jobs at the co-op would shrink. Jen, who does our rota, has been there eleven years, and a computer could do her job in a morning. I'd fight for her, but I'm not sure I'd win.

say: Carers are **fine**, so everyone should calm down a bit.
Money saved by software should go into **wages**, not a fancy office.
think: My job is **hands and kettles**, so the robots are years off for me.
Sam's **teaching assistant** job is the one that could shrink, and rent takes two wages.
do: Learn the new **rota and notes** system well enough to teach it.
Put a **motion** to the co-op meeting for paid travel time.
Draw up a **cut list** with Sam in case his hours drop.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching change reach Sam's school before his own work.
S1.quote: My job is hands and kettles, so the robots are years off for me, but our rent is two wages, not one.
fieldNote: His **public calm** hides worry about his partner's school job.
He'd become the **trainer** on new software rather than resist it.
He names Jen, the **rota coordinator**, as the person he'd fight for and might lose.

steps.text: Learn the new rota and notes system and teach it to new starters
Put a motion to the co-op for paid travel time from software savings
Agree a cut list with Sam, starting with the gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what governments exist for, and they'd better act like it. At the co-op I'd say we need to talk about robots before a big company turns up with a fleet of them. I'd be loud about it, but I'd try not to frighten the clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think both of us go. Sam's job looks shaky by 2028, when AI can teach a child to read, and mine by 2031, when a robot can do a bath. I'm twenty-seven with three weeks of savings, so that's not a plan, it's a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd ask the co-op to look at whether we could buy robots ourselves, so carers own them instead of being replaced by someone else's. I'd join the campaign for a public income for people pushed out of work, and write to our MP, our member of parliament. And Sam and I would cut right back and stop pretending we'd ever save a deposit for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. And angry that it's arriving before anybody has a plan for people like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the timing change for your work, with thinking AI in 2028 and robots about three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, 2028 is the paperwork going and maybe the rota, which honestly wouldn't hurt me much. The hands-on part has three more years. But those three years would be Sam out of work and me carrying the rent alone, waiting for my turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop pretending about the house. What did you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little terrace in the village with a yard for a dog. We used to look at them online on Sunday nights. I think in this picture we'd stop looking, because it would just make us sad.

say: This is exactly what **governments** exist for, and they'd better act.
The co-op must talk about **robots** before a big company arrives with a fleet.
think: Sam's job goes by **2028** and mine by **2031**.
With three weeks of savings, it's **a countdown**, not a plan.
do: Ask the co-op to look at **owning robots** so carers keep a share.
Join the campaign for a **public income** and write to the MP.
Cut right back and give up on a **house deposit**.
feel: **Scared** properly, and **angry** that nobody has a plan for people like him.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven with three weeks of savings, so robots by 2031 aren't a plan, they're a countdown.
fieldNote: He expects **both household earners** to lose their jobs within three years of each other.
His instinct is **collective ownership** of robots rather than fighting them.
Giving up on the **village terrace** shows how far his hopes would shrink.

steps.text: Ask the co-op to study buying robots that carers own
Join the campaign for a public income and write to the MP
Cut back hard and stop saving for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if people start now. I'd tell the co-op we should be training people for the jobs next to the robots, not hoping they never come. And I'd tell Sam's school the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it gives us a fighting chance. Robots by 2034 means I'd be thirty-five, still young enough to switch. I don't trust things until I've seen them work, though, so I'd want proof before I bet everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the dementia specialist course the health board runs, because people who know dementia deeply will be needed to set up and watch over any robot care. I'd start using the AI tools properly, not just now and then, so I'm not the one left behind. And we'd put Sam's Spanish class money into savings instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but less trapped. Like being told the exam is in five years instead of next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want proof first. What would count as proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing a robot help someone with dementia without frightening them. I've watched people panic at a new carer's face, never mind a machine. If I saw that work in a trial somewhere, I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the course on three weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The health board course is free if the co-op releases you a day a month, so I'd push for that. If it costs anything, I'd do extra weekend shifts. I've done worse for less.

say: **Five years** is enough to do this properly if people start now.
Train people for **jobs next to the robots**, not hope they never come.
think: Robots by **2034** leave me young enough to switch.
I won't bet everything until I've seen **proof** it works.
do: Sign up for the free **dementia specialist** course with the health board.
Start using **AI tools** properly instead of now and then.
Move the Spanish class money into **savings**.
feel: **Nervous** but less trapped, like an exam moved from next week to five years away.
S3.quote: If I saw a robot help someone with dementia without frightening them, I'd believe the robots can do this job.
fieldNote: His bar for proof is **concrete**: a robot calming a frightened dementia client.
He plans a **specialist route** to stay useful beside the machines.
Money still limits him; he'd rely on **free training** and extra weekend shifts.

steps.text: Take the free dementia specialist course with a day off a month
Use AI tools daily for notes and family messages
Move Sam's Spanish class money into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it arguing about whether it's real. At the co-op I'd push for a ten-year plan, which sounds very grand for a group of carers in a valley. Online I'd stay quiet until I knew more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd breathe out. Robots by 2039 means I'd be forty, with time to train for something on the health side that needs a person. I'd still be skint, but skint with a plan feels different from skint with a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the dementia round for now, because it pays the rent and I love it. I'd start a part-time occupational therapy degree in a couple of years, once I'd seen what the first AI changes did to the health jobs. And I'd keep going to the co-op meetings to make sure we plan for robots instead of being surprised by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. It's on my mind, not on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why occupational therapy, and why wait a couple of years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Occupational therapists help people stay independent at home, which is what I do now, but with more say over the plan. I'd wait because I want to see which health jobs AI hits first. No point in a four-year degree that's obsolete before I finish it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the thinking part of your job in 2036 and the hands-on part in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2036 the notes, the rota and the medicine checks would go to AI, and I'd be glad of the time. The baths and the walks to the bus stop last until 2039. By then I'd want to be the one writing the plan the robot follows.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, so don't waste it arguing about whether it's real.
The co-op needs a **ten-year plan**, however grand that sounds.
think: Robots by **2039** give me time to train for a health job that needs a person.
Skint with **a plan** feels different from skint with a countdown.
do: Keep the **dementia round** because it pays the rent.
Start a part-time **occupational therapy** degree in about two years.
Keep pushing the co-op to **plan for robots**.
feel: **Uneasy** but bearable: on his mind, not on his chest.
S4.quote: I'd still be skint, but skint with a plan feels different from skint with a countdown.
fieldNote: He waits for **evidence** before committing to a degree, true to his steady style.
He'd aim to **write the plan** robots follow, not compete with them.
Ten years turns his **countdown** into a manageable worry.

steps.text: Keep the dementia round while studying
Start a part-time occupational therapy degree around 2028
Push the co-op meeting to adopt a ten-year robot plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes Sam's job first and then mine, with no time between. What would help is a public income for people pushed out, and free training paid for while you study, not just courses you have to fit around a full rota.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what clients would want. Most of mine would hate a robot, but one or two might like not having a stranger see them undressed. Care is more complicated than people think, and I'd want those people asked too.

headlineQuote: Most of my clients would hate a robot, but one or two might like not having a stranger see them undressed.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old senior carer** on a rural dementia round for a carer-owned co-op.
He and his boyfriend Sam, a **teaching assistant**, have about three weeks of savings.
He uses AI **now and then** and wants proof before he bets on anything new.
His fear peaks in **AGI by 2028**, when both household jobs could go within three years.
With more time he plans **specialist training** and occupational therapy, and wants carers to own the robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Sam's job goes first and then his, with no time between.
whatWouldHelp: A **public income** for people pushed out of work.
**Paid training** while studying, not courses squeezed around a full rota.
